summary:
Astronauts face health hazards during long-range space missions, such as Mars missions. They need a way to track their health during the mission. The best way to do that is by using software. ASTRA is an astronaut health monitoring software made to track an astronaut’s health by values and trends of sensor data and data inputted by astronauts. It also contains an in-built Mars mission with 3 hazard windows to test the system’s functionality and a knowledge base with information about how space affects an astronaut’s health.

Even though ASTRA is not a system that can be used in real missions, it can be still used for education purposes and simulation purposes. Further development of this software can lead to a high-level software that can be used in future space missions. ASTRA issues alerts and notifications based on both astronaut-inputted and sensor values. Therefore, it minimizes human errors in data input. The sensor input system also let astronaut concentrate on their mission goals rather than spending a long time on entering data. This project uses data from NASA and CSA.
details:
ASTRA- Astronaut Health & Mission Simulation Console


Problem Identification

Contrary to what most people believe, the most challenging part of a crewed space mission is not planning the spaceship's path or programming the mission computers. Instead, it is managing astronauts' health during a mission. Research concluded by NASA states that Radiation, Isolation, Weightlessness, Distance from Earth, and Hostile environments affect both the mental and physical health of astronauts if not monitored and treated properly. Monitoring them manually is extremely inefficient and may lead to inaccurate conclusions. That motivated us to design software that will do that.

What is ASTRA?

ASTRA uses data collected from sensors that are attached to astronauts' spacesuits, cabin environment sensors, and manual data input by astronauts to determine the health status of an astronaut. The system also issues warning/alerts based on the urgency and severity of the health problem by 2 levels,

  1. Alert- Moderate urgency/no immediate danger, take appropriate action
  2. HIGH- High urgency/high health risk, take immediate action
How the application works?

As mentioned previously the system uses values from sensors and astronauts' data input. But, this application is not currently connected to any physical sensors. Instead, it work on sensor values we provide to the system. The system has 2 main modes,

  1. Manual Input- The sensor values and environmental variables can be adjusted as needed using the "Sensor Lab" menu of the mission console. The software responds according to the data we enter.
  2. Earth-Mars mission- The mission is divided into 1000 data points; each data point outputs sensor readings accordingly. To simulate the functions of our software, we have planned 3 health hazard windows in the mission: A solar flare event, a crew well being anomaly , and a cabin anomaly.

The following interface shows how values and warnings are displayed in the software.

However in both modes, astronauts can manually enter data about their health using "Crew Logs & Records" option. But, for the Mars mission, some values like sleep, calorie intake, exercise hours, and fatigue level are pre-planned to match the project phrase.

The simulated Earth to Mars missionTo brief our software, we have added a simulated Mars mission, as mentioned before, with animations. The simulation speed can be controlled using relevant sliders, and the bottom strip shows 3 health hazard windows of the mission. Further down in the same menu, it displays sensor values and cabin environmental values for the given timestamp.

In the "Crew Resilience" dashboard, the user can view a summarized chart of each sensor value/data for each indicator throughout the whole mission. The indicator can be chosen from the given dropdown menu.

Using the "Mission Debrief" menu, users can generate a debrief for a certain crew member for the whole mission or a certain part of the mission.

The knowledge base

The knowledge base contains information about how space missions may affect astronauts' health conditions. It contains real research data and published data by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA)

Impact, benefits of the project and future developments

  • The system continuously monitors astronauts' health during a mission. Therefore, the astronaut will be notified if an anomaly is detected, and he can take action accordingly.
  • Our simulator simulates different stages of a Mars mission. It helps researchers evaluate whether astronaut monitoring systems can remain useful throughout different mission stages.
  • ASTRA's knowledge base uses real research evidence, so it can be strongly used for educational purposes related to Space Health.
Scientific and educational impact
  • Demonstrate how software engineering, astronomy, medicine, and space science work together.
  • Makes a complex Mars mission scenario easier to understand.
  • Provides a platform for students and researchers to experiment with simulated astronaut health data.
Future developments
  • AI-powered software can be used to identify diseases by symptoms and suggest treatments.
  • The data inputs can be integrated with real-time wearable devices such as space vests and watches.
  • Radiation level determination can be integrated with space weather data provided by the Space Weather Prediction Centre of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

The vision of our project "ASTRA" is,

"Creating an integrated astronaut health and mission support ecosystem for future human space exploration."

The software is fully developed using Python, and it uses the libraries streamlit (runs the web and application interface), numpy (handles tables and data processing), and pandas (Runs numerical calculations and data operations). Inside the Python files, we have also used HTML, Base64, JSON, and SQLite.
